GEMS: Molecular Structure Elucidation as Learned Search over Isomer Graphs

Utku Umur Acikalin Affiliation: Department of Computer Science, Cornell University    Yingheng Wang Affiliation: Department of Computer Science, Cornell University    Goncalo J. Gouveia Affiliation: Department of Chemistry and Chemical Biology, Cornell University Affiliation: Boyce Thompson Institute, Cornell University    Tyler J. Schwertfeger Affiliation: Department of Chemistry and Chemical Biology, Cornell University Affiliation: Boyce Thompson Institute, Cornell University    Frank C. Schroeder Affiliation: Department of Chemistry and Chemical Biology, Cornell University Affiliation: Boyce Thompson Institute, Cornell University    Carla P. Gomes Affiliation: Department of Computer Science, Cornell University
Abstract

Identifying small-molecule structures from molecular formulas and tandem mass spectra remains a bottleneck in untargeted metabolomics and natural-product discovery. Even when database retrieval or de novo prediction does not identify the exact molecular structure, the resulting candidates can provide starting points for exploring nearby structures through a few bond edits. We introduce GEMS (Guided Editing of Molecular Structures), which refines candidates through learned 2-switch bond edits that preserve the molecular formula and each atom’s total valence. Molecular fingerprints encode local structural features and can be computed directly from candidate structures. GEMS uses MIST, a pretrained spectrum-to-fingerprint model, to predict fingerprint probabilities once per spectrum. A neural policy compares each candidate’s fingerprint with these predictions, links present features to the atoms and bonds that generate them, and scores all valid edits in one forward pass. The policy is trained on shortest edit paths between structures, so it can be pretrained on PubChem isomers without spectra and then fine-tuned with spectrum-predicted fingerprints. At inference, GEMS searches from multiple initial candidates matching the supplied molecular formula and ranks candidates by fingerprint agreement and multi-start consensus. With the target structure excluded from PubChem initialization, three edit rounds achieve Hit@1/Hit@10 of 29.64%/50.81% on NPLIB1 and 30.22%/41.33% on MassSpecGym, exceeding published baselines under comparable settings. On NPLIB1, GEMS achieves higher identification accuracy in about 3.3 minutes end to end, compared with 26.2 hours for our FRIGID run. GEMS also improves identification from generated candidates, including those refined by FRIGID. Experiments with exact target fingerprints identify fingerprint prediction error as a bottleneck in target recovery and final ranking. Deeper search recovers additional targets without retraining, with larger gains from weaker initial candidates.

1 Introduction

Identifying unknown small molecules is a central challenge in untargeted metabolomics and natural-product discovery. Many measured spectra remain unassigned to structures, limiting what experiments reveal about a sample’s chemistry (Bushuiev et al., 2024). Tandem mass spectrometry (MS/MS) measures the mass-to-charge ratios and intensities of fragment ions, providing clues about substructures whose arrangement can remain ambiguous. We study the known-formula setting, which fixes elemental composition while leaving connectivity to be determined. Even then, many isomers can be consistent with the observed spectrum.

Database retrieval ranks existing structures, so success requires the target to be in the database (Dührkop et al., 2015; Goldman et al., 2023). Generative methods can propose new structures, but recovering exact connectivity remains difficult (Stravs et al., 2022; Bohde et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2026). Yet even when these methods miss the target, their candidates are often only a few bond edits away. For each NPLIB1 spectrum, we remove the target from PubChem and retrieve up to five isomers whose fingerprints best match the one predicted from the spectrum. For at least 72.85% of spectra, one of these isomers lies within three bond edits of the target (Appendix I.2). FRIGID, a recent de novo method (Bohde et al., 2026), shows a similar pattern in its initial candidate pool: among spectra with no correct selected starting candidate, at least 47.79% have a starting candidate within three bond edits of the target (Appendix H.3).

These near misses suggest correcting candidates locally rather than discarding them. Two recent methods do this with ICEBERG, a structure-to-spectrum model (Goldman et al., 2024). FRIGID remasks and regenerates candidate regions (Bohde et al., 2026), and FOAM mutates candidates and selects them by predicted spectra (Manjrekar et al., 2026). We instead supply candidate–fingerprint correspondences directly to a learned policy, which learns to select bond edits from this evidence without simulating spectra.

We introduce GEMS (Guided Editing of Molecular Structures), which formulates structure elucidation as learned search over molecular isomers (Figure 1). Each search step applies a 2-switch edit, which removes one bond unit from each of two bonds and reconnects their endpoints. One bond may be to a hydrogen. These edits preserve the molecular formula and each atom’s total valence. MIST, a pretrained spectrum-to-fingerprint model, predicts the target fingerprint probabilities once per spectrum (Goldman et al., 2023). The policy compares these probabilities with the candidate’s fingerprint and links the candidate’s present features to their generating atoms and bonds. A present feature with low predicted probability, for example, points to where an edit may help. A candidate can admit hundreds or thousands of valid edits, all scored in one forward pass without fingerprinting every possible product. GEMS runs beam searches from several initial candidates, then ranks the retained molecules by fingerprint agreement and by how many independent searches reach them.

We train the policy on shortest edit paths between molecular structures. Several edits can be equally good first steps toward the target, so rather than picking one as the label, we maximize the total probability of all edits that begin a shortest path. Both this supervision and the exact target fingerprint can be computed from structures alone, so we pretrain the policy on pairs of PubChem isomers without any spectra, then fine-tune it on benchmark training spectra with MIST-predicted fingerprints. Because the best next edit depends only on the current molecule and the target, the policy is Markovian: its inputs, including the fingerprint correspondence, are computed from the current molecule and predicted fingerprint, with no trajectory history or depth index. The same policy can therefore search at greater depths and refine retrieved or generated candidates without retraining or changing the generator architecture.

Our contributions are: (1) We formulate known-formula structure elucidation as search over an isomer graph whose edges are formula- and valence-preserving 2-switch edits, allowing retrieved or generated candidates to be corrected locally. Because one close start is enough, we search from several starts, and even a simple Enumerate & Score (E&S) search, which scores every valid one-edit product by fingerprint agreement without a learned policy, matches or exceeds the compared published baselines on the same splits in Hit@1 and Hit@10. (2) We introduce GEMS, whose policy links present fingerprint features to the atoms and bonds that generate them and scores all valid edits in one forward pass. Even from PubChem starts that exclude every isomer with Tanimoto similarity of at least 0.7 to the target, GEMS exceeds all Table 1 baselines in Hit@1 and Hit@10 on both datasets. It ranks more targets first than E&S at matched width, and outperforms it at wider width with 13–21-fold lower runtime. From FRIGID’s initial NPLIB1 candidates, without database retrieval, GEMS also outperforms FRIGID’s refinement of the same pool. (3) We introduce a pretraining strategy that uses all shortest edit paths between pairs of structures as supervision, so it requires no spectra. A policy pretrained only on PubChem isomers, without training on any spectra, already exceeds all Table 1 baselines on NPLIB1 in Hit@1 and Hit@10 (28.89% Hit@1). When both are trained from scratch on experimental NPLIB1 spectra, this supervision also outperforms REINFORCE with exact-fingerprint rewards. (4) We study how start quality, search width and depth, and fingerprint accuracy shape recovery and identification. Deeper search helps most from weak starts but raises recovery more than identification, while exact fingerprints improve both.

2 Related Work

Candidate ranking.

CSI:FingerID and MIST predict molecular fingerprints from MS/MS spectra to rank database candidates (Dührkop et al., 2015; Goldman et al., 2023). Other approaches, including CFM-ID, ICEBERG, MassFormer, FraGNNet, GLACIER, and AIMe, use spectrum prediction to support ranking by spectral similarity (Allen et al., 2014; Goldman et al., 2024; Young et al., 2024; Young et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026; Acikalin et al., 2026). These approaches rank a supplied candidate set. GEMS uses MIST retrieval to select starting structures, then edits their connectivity to explore additional isomers.

De novo generation.

MSNovelist, Spec2Mol, and MS2Mol generate molecular strings from spectra or predicted fingerprints (Stravs et al., 2022; Litsa et al., 2023; Butler et al., 2023). DiffMS and MBGen generate molecular graphs through diffusion, while FlowMS uses discrete flow matching (Bohde et al., 2025; Sun et al., 2026; Nie and Gao, 2026). All three use MIST encoders and pretrain their decoders on fingerprint–structure pairs. FRIGID-base (without ICEBERG refinement) and MS-GPT generate SAFE strings, a fragment-based molecular representation, from predicted fingerprints through masked diffusion and autoregressive decoding, respectively (Bohde et al., 2026; Zhao et al., 2026). MS-GPT handles fingerprint uncertainty through multiple calibrated binary queries. Generated structures can initialize GEMS, which explores additional isomers through learned bond edits.

Scaffold conditioning and candidate refinement.

MADGEN completes a retrieved scaffold, while MSAnchor predicts a scaffold and its attachment sites to guide generation (Wang et al., 2025; Qin et al., 2026). FRIGID refines complete candidates using ICEBERG fragment predictions (Bohde et al., 2026; Goldman et al., 2024). It uses discrepancies between a candidate’s predicted fragments and the experimental spectrum to set masking probabilities through a fixed rule, and its learned diffusion model then regenerates the masked regions from the predicted fingerprint and formula, without explicitly receiving the discrepancy information. FOAM searches from retrieved or generated structures through random formula-preserving mutations and crossovers, and uses ICEBERG-predicted spectra, together with a structural-complexity penalty, only to select candidates (Manjrekar et al., 2026). GEMS learns to select valid bond edits from candidate–fingerprint correspondences, using the same MIST fingerprint prediction throughout search, without simulating candidate spectra.

Molecular graph editing.

Chemical graph enumeration has a long history, from DENDRAL to Surge (Lindsay et al., 1993; McKay et al., 2022), and learned graph edits have also been used for chemical reaction prediction (Do et al., 2019). GEMS builds on classical degree-preserving 2-switches (Senior, 1951; Hakimi, 1962; Taylor, 1981; Fernandes, 2022), adapting them to molecular bonds and attached hydrogens and learning which valid edits to apply from spectral evidence.

3 Structure Elucidation as Search over Isomers

3.1 Molecular Candidates and Bond Edits

We represent each candidate by its heavy atoms, integer bond orders, and each heavy atom’s hydrogen count. We consider connected, neutral molecules without isotopic labels or radicals, and evaluate connectivity with stereochemistry removed. Each search step applies a formula-preserving bond edit.

We use two types of 2-switch edits (Figure 2), where a bond unit is one bond-order unit. Type-A removes one bond unit from each of two heavy-atom bonds, (u,v)(u,v) and (w,z)(w,z), with four distinct atoms, and adds one unit each to (u,w)(u,w) and (v,z)(v,z). The other pairing adds (u,z)(u,z) and (v,w)(v,w) instead.

Type-B uses the same switch with a hydrogen endpoint. Let uu, vv, and ww be distinct heavy atoms, with a hydrogen on uu and a bond between vv and ww. The edit removes the uu–H bond, reduces the vv–ww bond order by one, adds a uu–vv bond unit, and attaches the hydrogen to ww. Exchanging vv and ww gives the other pairing. For example, keto–enol interconversion can be represented by one Type-B edit.

In both edit types, every affected atom loses and gains one bond unit. The edits therefore preserve the formula and each atom’s total bond order, including attached hydrogens. We retain products with nonnegative integer bond orders up to three, nonnegative attached-hydrogen counts, and a connected heavy-atom graph. Appendix A.1 gives the matrix representation and invariants.

3.2 Search over Isomers

Applying a valid edit produces another candidate with the same molecular formula. These transitions define an implicit isomer graph 𝒢ℱ=(𝒱ℱ,ℰℱ)\mathcal{G}_{\mathcal{F}}=(\mathcal{V}_{\mathcal{F}},\mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{F}}). Each node is a molecular state as defined in Section 3.1 with formula ℱ\mathcal{F}, and an edge corresponds to a valid edit between two states. A sequence of edits traces a path through this graph. The edits also preserve each atom’s total valence, so sharing a molecular formula does not guarantee that two states can be connected by a path of valid edits.

We enumerate outgoing edits only when expanding a state. For EE heavy-atom bond units and nn heavy atoms, there are O⁡(E2)O(E^{2}) potential Type-A and O⁡(n​E)O(nE) potential Type-B edits, each checked for validity. Rapid neighborhood growth (Appendix K.3) motivates learned beam search that selects edits before fingerprinting their products.

3.3 Candidate Recovery and Ranking

Search starts from initial isomers and returns a pool of candidate structures. It reaches the target when the pool contains a structure with the target’s InChIKey14, the first 14 characters of the InChIKey. GEMS can fail at three stages. Initialization may supply no candidate from which the target is reachable within the search depth. Search may discard a path to the target. Ranking may place other candidates above a recovered target. We examine initialization and depth in Section 5.5, and fingerprint errors in navigation and ranking in Section 5.6.

4 GEMS

At each step, the candidate molecule specifies present local structural features and their locations. Fingerprint probabilities predicted from the experimental spectrum indicate the unknown target’s likely features. The navigation policy uses their agreement and discrepancies to choose bond edits.

Given a spectrum SS and molecular formula ℱ\mathcal{F}, GEMS uses MIST, a frozen spectrum-to-fingerprint model, to predict q∈[0,1]4096q\in[0,1]^{4096}. These probabilities are computed once and remain fixed throughout search. GEMS selects initial isomers, searches from each independently, and ranks the retained candidates by fingerprint agreement and support from distinct starts:

q\displaystyle q =gMIST​(S,ℱ),\displaystyle=g_{\mathrm{MIST}}(S,\mathcal{F}), (1)
ℳ0\displaystyle\mathcal{M}_{0} =ℐ⁡(q,ℱ),\displaystyle=\mathcal{I}(q,\mathcal{F}),
𝒞θ\displaystyle\mathcal{C}_{\theta} =Searchθ⁡(q,ℳ0,𝒢ℱ),\displaystyle=\operatorname{Search}_{\theta}(q,\mathcal{M}_{0},\mathcal{G}_{\mathcal{F}}),
m^\displaystyle\widehat{m} =arg⁡maxm∈𝒞θ⁡R⁡(m,q).\displaystyle=\arg\max_{m\in\mathcal{C}_{\theta}}R(m;q).

4.1 Initialization

GEMS starts from chemically valid molecules with formula ℱ\mathcal{F}. These can come from database retrieval or a de novo generator such as FRIGID (Bohde et al., 2026) or MS-GPT (Zhao et al., 2026). Our main configuration selects initial PubChem isomers by agreement with the predicted fingerprint.

For a candidate fingerprint x⁡(m)∈{0,1}4096x(m)\in\{0,1\}^{4096}, we measure agreement with qq using the independent-bit Bernoulli log likelihood

s⁡(m,q)=∑i[xi​(m)​log⁡q~i+(1−xi​(m))​log⁡(1−q~i)],s(m;q)=\sum_{i}\bigl[x_{i}(m)\log\widetilde{q}_{i}+(1-x_{i}(m))\log(1-\widetilde{q}_{i})\bigr], (2)

where q~i=clip⁡(qi,10−7,1−10−7)\widetilde{q}_{i}=\operatorname{clip}(q_{i},10^{-7},1-10^{-7}). This score is used for both retrieval and final ranking.

We rank PubChem molecules with formula ℱ\mathcal{F} by s⁡(m,q)s(m;q), retain the highest-scoring representative of each InChIKey14 group, and select up to K=5K=5{} initial structures. In target-excluded evaluation, we remove the target InChIKey14 group before selecting the starts. A correct prediction therefore requires at least one edit to a retrieved structure.

4.2 Candidate–Fingerprint Correspondence

GEMS compares the candidate’s radius-two, 4,096-bit Morgan fingerprint x⁡(m)x(m) (Rogers and Hahn, 2010) with the spectrum-predicted probabilities qq (Figure 1b). Supported present bits occur in the candidate and have high qiq_{i}, while unsupported present bits occur in the candidate and have low qiq_{i}. Likely missing bits are absent from the candidate but have high qiq_{i}. Together, they suggest which features to preserve, change, or introduce.

An atom environment comprises a center atom and surrounding atoms and bonds within zero, one, or two bond steps. For each present fingerprint bit, we retain all environments that generate it, linking the bit to the candidate’s atoms and bonds. In Figure 1(b), bit 3480 is present in Seed 5 and corresponds to a radius-one environment centered on its carbonyl carbon, but has predicted probability below 0.001. The policy uses this localized evidence to score edits. Missing bits have no corresponding environment in the candidate, but still provide target evidence through their fingerprint tokens.

The policy receives 128 fingerprint tokens, initially allocated as 48 likely missing, 48 unsupported present, and 32 supported present bits (Appendix C). Each encodes bit identity, role, qiq_{i}, xix_{i}, and uncertainty and discrepancy features.

4.3 Fingerprint-Conditioned Navigation Policy

A transformer encodes the fingerprint tokens, and a Graphormer-style molecular encoder (Ying et al., 2021) processes the candidate. Atom representations attend to fingerprint tokens with learned biases distinguishing environment centers, other members, and atoms outside the environment. Directed-bond representations are then constructed from atom representations and bond features. They attend to fingerprint tokens using separate biases that describe whether a bond and its endpoints belong to an environment. These connections let the policy associate predicted fingerprint support with the atoms and bonds involved in an edit. Appendix D.2 gives the layer arrangement.

Each valid edit is scored from the representations of the atoms and bonds it changes. We concatenate the relevant representations with action-type and global molecular features and combine them using multilayer perceptrons. The same edit can be written with its endpoints in different orders. To make its score independent of these equivalent orderings, we average their action representations before projecting to a logit. A softmax over the valid edit set 𝒜⁡(m)\mathcal{A}(m) gives

pθ​(a∣m,q,ℱ)=softmaxa∈𝒜⁡(m)⁡ℓθ​(a,m,q,ℱ).p_{\theta}(a\mid m,q,\mathcal{F})=\operatorname{softmax}_{a\in\mathcal{A}(m)}\ell_{\theta}(a;m,q,\mathcal{F}). (3)

One forward pass scores all valid edits. Product molecules are constructed and fingerprinted only for actions selected by search. The Markovian policy conditions on the current molecule, fingerprint probabilities, and formula, without trajectory history or a depth index.

4.4 Training the Navigation Policy

During training, the chosen target graph tt is known. We identify edits that move a source molecule mm one step closer to tt along a shortest valid path. Several edits may be equally good: if three edits are required, every first edit that leaves a two-edit path to tt is optimal. Let 𝒜+​(m,t)\mathcal{A}^{+}(m;t) contain all such optimal first edits. We maximize their total probability by minimizing

ℒnav=−log∑a∈𝒜+​(m,t)pθ(a∣m,q,ℱ).\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{nav}}=-\log\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}^{+}(m;t)}p_{\theta}(a\mid m,q,\mathcal{F}). (4)

This objective does not require choosing a single optimal edit as the label. In Figure 1(b), Seed 5’s four highest-ranked edits each begin a shortest three-edit path and jointly receive 96.4% of policy probability. Dkk denotes sources whose shortest valid path to the chosen target graph tt has kk edits.11 1 Training paths exclude held-out structures and match the chosen target graph up to atom renumbering. Evaluation accepts any structure with the target’s InChIKey14, so evaluation distances can be shorter (Appendix A.2).

Structure-only pretraining first teaches the policy to navigate with exact target fingerprints. Fine-tuning then adapts it to fingerprints predicted by a frozen MIST encoder from experimental spectra.

PubChem pretraining.

We mine PubChem isomer pairs one or two edits apart and keep all optimal first edits for each. The input is the exact target fingerprint, q=x⁡(t)q=x(t), so no spectra are needed. If each source had a single target, the policy could learn a molecule’s typical edits and ignore the fingerprint. Half the examples therefore come in groups that share a source but have different targets, preferably with different optimal edits, encouraging the policy to use the target fingerprint. The other half selects one pair per sampled source group to cover more formulas and molecules. Both benchmark models start from one shared checkpoint, selected on validation after 37.5 million examples (Appendix D).

Fine-tuning with predicted fingerprints.

Fine-tuning pairs benchmark training targets with same-formula PubChem sources one to three edits away, using fingerprint probabilities predicted from the target’s spectrum by the frozen MIST encoder. It varies the source for a fixed target, complementing the fixed-source, varying-target groups in pretraining. We find shortest paths by meeting in the middle: the target is expanded by up to two edits, each source by one, and the neighborhoods are matched. Targets above 35 heavy atoms use D1 and D2 only, because two-step expansion is costly. We keep all available D1 and D2 observations and a capped number of D3 sources per spectrum, selected by MIST Bernoulli agreement to approximate how starting candidates are selected at inference (Appendix B).

4.5 Multi-Start Policy Beam Search

GEMS runs an independent beam search from each of KK initial structures, with proposal width PP, beam width BB, and maximum depth DD. Our main setting uses K=5K=5{}, P=16P=16{}, B=16B=16{}, and D=3D=3{}. For a trajectory πd=(m0,a1,m1,…,ad,md)\pi_{d}=(m_{0},a_{1},m_{1},\ldots,a_{d},m_{d}), the score is the cumulative policy log probability:

Lθ​(πd,q,ℱ)=∑t=1dlog⁡pθ​(at∣mt−1,q,ℱ).L_{\theta}(\pi_{d};q,\mathcal{F})=\sum_{t=1}^{d}\log p_{\theta}(a_{t}\mid m_{t-1},q,\mathcal{F}). (5)

At each depth, the policy scores all valid edits from each beam state. We construct product molecules and compute their fingerprints only for the top PP selected actions. Within each start’s search, previously visited products are removed, and duplicate products retain their highest-scoring trajectory. The top BB trajectories under LθL_{\theta} form the next beam. The visited set records all proposed products, including those outside the next beam (Algorithm 1, Appendix E).

The final candidate pool contains the initial structures and beam states retained at every depth across all starts. With our main setting, search uses at most K⁡[1+B⁡(D−1)]=165K[1+B(D-1)]=165{} state-level policy evaluations and retains at most K⁡(1+B​D)=245K(1+BD)=245{} states before final deduplication.

4.6 Final Ranking by Fingerprint Evidence and Consensus

Searches from different seeds can reach the same molecule. This agreement is an additional ranking signal. Let c⁡(m)c(m) count the distinct seeds whose retained search pools contain mm, including the seeds themselves. Each seed contributes at most one vote. In Figure 1(c), candidate A receives five votes and candidate C receives three, including a vote because C is Seed 1’s initial structure. Support merges atom renumberings and alternative Kekulé assignments while keeping tautomers distinct (Appendix A.3).

The final score is R⁡(m,q)=s⁡(m,q)+λ​log⁡(1+c⁡(m))R(m;q)=s(m;q)+\lambda\log(1+c(m)), where s⁡(m,q)s(m;q) measures fingerprint agreement and λ\lambda weights consensus. We use λ=16\lambda=16{} for both benchmarks, selected on MassSpecGym validation. We retain each InChIKey14 group’s highest-scoring candidate and rank these representatives by R⁡(m,q)R(m;q).

5 Experiments

5.1 Setup and Evaluation

Datasets and metrics.

We use the same NPLIB1 split as FRIGID, with 803 protonated test spectra (Dührkop et al., 2021; Bohde et al., 2026), and the structurally held-out MassSpecGym split with all 17,556 test spectra, 14,066 protonated and 3,490 sodiated (Bushuiev et al., 2024). One MassSpecGym policy serves both adducts. Hit@kk measures correctness among the first kk ranked connectivities. All queries contribute to accuracy and reach, including 17 NPLIB1 and 200 MassSpecGym queries without starts. MassSpecGym hit counts are pooled across adducts.

Comparisons.

Published baselines come from FRIGID Table 1 and MassSpecGym in the Wild Table 9 (Bohde et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026). Appendix F.2 reports MS-GPT’s published results and our best-effort reproduction with corrected masking and retraining on the same benchmark splits.

5.2 Main Results

GEMS achieves the highest Hit@1 and Hit@10 in Table 1 on both benchmarks. Relative to the strongest baseline, FRIGID on NPLIB1 and our MS-GPT reproduction on MassSpecGym, the gains are 4.61/17.44 and 6.99/13.63 percentage points. Because PubChem starts exclude the target connectivity, every hit requires at least one edit.

GEMS also has the highest Top-10 Tanimoto similarity among these methods: 0.71 versus 0.64 for FRIGID on NPLIB1, and 0.61 versus 0.53 (FOAM) on MassSpecGym. MCES results are mixed across benchmarks and ranks, with full comparisons in Appendix F.2.

With starts of Tanimoto similarity ≥0.7\geq 0.7 to the target also excluded, GEMS still exceeds every baseline in Table 1 in Hit@1 and Hit@10 on both benchmarks (Appendix H.2).

5.3 Refining Generator Initializations

GEMS refines generated candidates without retraining (Table 10). From the NPLIB1 FRIGID-base pool, it raises Hit@1/Hit@10 of the selected starts from 20.42%/23.91% to 28.02%/43.34%, above 24.03%/33.13% for our FRIGID run after 24 ICEBERG refinement rounds, and those of FRIGID’s final pool from 22.54%/30.14% to 28.27%/46.82%. For our MS-GPT reproduction, it raises Hit@1 from 21.05% to 26.28% on NPLIB1 and from 23.23% to 25.56% on MassSpecGym (Appendix H.3).

5.4 Learned Proposals Enable Wider Search

We compare learned proposals with Enumerate & Score (E&S) from the same five MIST-ranked, target-excluded starts. E&S constructs and fingerprints every valid one-edit neighbor, retaining the best BB trajectories per start by fingerprint log likelihood. Both methods search three edits deep and rank retained candidates with λ=16\lambda=16. We test E&S widths B∈{1,2,4}B\in\{1,2,4\} and GEMS widths P=B∈{4,16}P=B\in\{4,16\} (Table 6). Every tested E&S width exceeds the published baselines in Table 1 in Hit@1 and Hit@10 on both benchmarks.

At width sixteen, GEMS exceeds all tested E&S widths in Hit@1, Hit@10, and reach on both benchmarks. Against E&S B=4B=4, NPLIB1 Hit@1/Hit@10 rises from 26.03%/49.07% to 29.64%/50.81%, and reach from 54.17% to 57.78%. MassSpecGym Hit@1 rises from 28.16% to 30.22% and reach from 44.24% to 46.88%. Learned proposals make the wider beam practical: GEMS takes 200.12 s on NPLIB1 versus 2,524.59 s for E&S (B=4B=4), a 12.62-fold difference. The MassSpecGym ratio is 21.36 (Appendix K).

Random-weight policies achieve 4.61±2.904.61\pm 2.90% NPLIB1 Hit@1 under the same proposal and beam budget (Appendix G.1).

5.5 Initialization, Search Width, and Depth

At depth three, up to five MIST-ranked starts from the same-formula PubChem pool reach 57.78% of NPLIB1 targets. Ranking within a random 250-isomer subset reaches 50.44%, and using five random starts reaches 22.17% (Table 7). At width sixteen, extending search from three to ten rounds adds 18.68 points of reach from up to five random starts but 2.12 points from full-pool MIST-ranked starts.

We next vary width and depth from up to five MIST-ranked starts or up to 100 random starts, keeping the checkpoint and each starting set fixed (Figure 4, Appendix I.1). From P=B=D=3P=B=D=3, widening to P=B=10P=B=10 at D=3D=3 and deepening to D=10D=10 at P=B=3P=B=3 each retain at most 30 search states plus the initial structure per start. Under MIST guidance, widening gives higher Hit@1 than deepening from ranked starts (29.89% versus 29.02%), while deepening gives higher Hit@1 from up to 100 random starts (29.39% versus 25.90%). With exact fingerprints, deepening helps more from both starting sets. Hit@10 and per-seed reach follow the same ordering. The relative benefits of width and depth therefore depend on initialization and fingerprint evidence.

With up to five MIST-ranked starts, D1–D2/D2–D3 adds 2.37/0.25 Hit@1 points on NPLIB1 and 0.34/−0.21-0.21 on MassSpecGym. Removing starts within one edit of the target makes D1 Hit@1 zero by construction; D2/D3 reaches 24.16%/25.53% and 20.31%/22.44%, respectively (Appendix H.2).

5.6 Fingerprint Errors Limit Search and Ranking

MIST fingerprints guide retrieval, navigation, and ranking. We keep the MIST-selected starts and trained checkpoint fixed and replace the navigation fingerprint, ranking fingerprint, or both with the exact target fingerprint. A ranking-only substitution preserves the retained pool and consensus counts.

On fixed candidate pools, exact-fingerprint ranking raises Hit@1 from 29.64% to 56.66% on NPLIB1 and from 30.22% to 45.12% on MassSpecGym (Figure 3), placing the target first for nearly all recovered queries. Exact navigation raises reach from 57.78% to 72.85% and from 46.88% to 56.07%, respectively. With MIST ranking, however, Hit@1 rises only to 33.25% and 33.82%. Fingerprint prediction error thus limits both recovery and final ranking (Appendix J). Reranking the top ten with an ICEBERG spectral score adds 2.24 and 1.38 Hit@1 points on the two benchmarks (Appendix J.3).

6 Discussion and Limitations

GEMS shows that local correction of complete candidates is effective for known-formula structure elucidation. Needing only same-formula structures and a predicted fingerprint, one policy refines retrieved candidates and outputs of generators with different architectures. It makes wider search practical and remains useful at greater depths with weak starts. The exact-fingerprint interventions point to better spectrum-to-fingerprint prediction as a route to better recovery and ranking.

The method assumes a known formula and evaluates connectivity without stereochemistry. Formula uncertainty would require searching and ranking across multiple formula hypotheses. The policy reflects its PubChem training data, PubChem initialization depends on available same-formula candidates, and valence-preserving edits restrict the states reachable from each start.

Ethics Statement

This work develops computational methods for molecular annotation in metabolomics and natural-product research. More accurate structure proposals may accelerate discovery, but predictions require experimental validation and should not be the sole evidence for safety-critical chemical identification.

AI Use Statement

Generative AI assisted implementation and debugging, experiment planning and coordination, analysis, literature search, and drafting and editing manuscript text. The authors tested the code, checked numerical results against experiment outputs and bibliographic claims against primary sources, and take responsibility for the final content.

Reproducibility Statement

Appendices A–E specify molecular states, supervision construction, model inputs, training, and search. Appendices F–K give full results, evaluation conventions, and timing boundaries. Upon publication, we will publicly release our code, trained GEMS checkpoints, and supporting artifacts, including experiment configurations, starting-candidate lists, and data-preparation scripts, to enable reproduction of the reported results.
