Appendix A Molecular States and Target Equivalence

A.1 Molecular Representation and Transition Invariants

A molecular state contains an ordered tuple of heavy-atom symbols and an integer adjacency matrix 𝐀\mathbf{A}. For i≠ji\neq j, Ai​j∈{0,1,2,3}A_{ij}\in\{0,1,2,3\} gives the bond multiplicity between heavy atoms ii and jj. The diagonal entry Ai​iA_{ii} gives the number of hydrogens attached to atom ii. Atom indices specify the endpoints affected by an individual edit. Every retained state is connected, neutral, non-isotopic, and non-radical. Stereochemistry is removed.

Proposition 1 (Transition invariants).

For every retained transition m′=T⁡(m,a)m^{\prime}=T(m,a) and aligned atom ii,

𝖿𝗈𝗋𝗆⁡(m′)=𝖿𝗈𝗋𝗆⁡(m),Ai​i′+∑j≠iAi​j′=Ai​i+∑j≠iAi​j.\mathsf{form}(m^{\prime})=\mathsf{form}(m),\qquad A^{\prime}_{ii}+\sum_{j\neq i}A^{\prime}_{ij}=A_{ii}+\sum_{j\neq i}A_{ij}. (6)

Thus each action preserves the molecular formula and the total bond order incident to every aligned atom.

The equalities follow from the balanced bond-unit subtraction and addition in both action types. The transition filter separately enforces supported bond orders and connectedness.

A.2 Training and Evaluation Target Equivalence

Let 𝒯train​(t)\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{train}}(t) contain the states isomorphic to the chosen target graph, preserving heavy-atom symbols, integer bond orders, and attached hydrogens. Atom numbering may differ, but a match must preserve the complete literal graph. The matching key preserves the chosen Kekulé assignment and tautomer. The evaluation target class is

𝒯eval​(t)={u∈𝒱ℱ:IK14⁡(u)=IK14⁡(t)}.\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{eval}}(t)=\{u\in\mathcal{V}_{\mathcal{F}}:\operatorname{IK14}(u)=\operatorname{IK14}(t)\}. (7)

The training class is contained in the evaluation class.

Write 𝒢ℱtrain\mathcal{G}_{\mathcal{F}}^{\mathrm{train}} for the edit graph restricted to states admitted by the training exclusions, including removal of held-out intermediates. For admitted sources and targets, define

dtrain​(s,t)\displaystyle d_{\mathrm{train}}(s,t) =minu∈𝒯train​(t)⁡d𝒢ℱtrain​(s,u),\displaystyle=\min_{u\in\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{train}}(t)}d_{\mathcal{G}_{\mathcal{F}}^{\mathrm{train}}}(s,u), (8)
deval​(s,t)\displaystyle d_{\mathrm{eval}}(s,t) =minu∈𝒯eval​(t)⁡d𝒢ℱ​(s,u).\displaystyle=\min_{u\in\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{eval}}(t)}d_{\mathcal{G}_{\mathcal{F}}}(s,u).

An unreachable target class has infinite distance. Every admissible training path is also an admissible evaluation path, and the evaluation goal is broader. Consequently,

deval​(s,t)≤dtrain​(s,t).d_{\mathrm{eval}}(s,t)\leq d_{\mathrm{train}}(s,t). (9)

A source can require three edits to reach the chosen training target and only two to reach another evaluation-equivalent structure.

A.3 Path Matching and Search Deduplication

Training joins use a canonical key for the literal integer-bond graph without aromatizing or changing its Kekulé assignment. A proposed match must admit an atom mapping that preserves the complete adjacency matrix and heavy-atom symbols. Target-side actions are reversed and transported through that mapping into the source coordinates. Each resulting forward action is checked against the valid edit set, intermediate exclusions are enforced, and the final state must match the reference target graph.

Online beam search and consensus use canonical stereo-free aromatic SMILES as a structural key. This key identifies alternative Kekulé assignments and keeps tautomers distinct. Search retains one concrete state for each selected key and applies subsequent edits to that state. Retaining one representation per key can discard distinct edit continuations. InChIKey14 is used for target exclusion and connectivity evaluation. Search paths consist of valid edits between concrete molecular states.

Appendix B Supervision Construction

B.1 Identity, Validity, and Held-Out Exclusion

Supervision and online search use the same action enumeration, application, and validation code. Appendix A defines the molecular states, matching rules, and identity conventions.

Before PubChem pretraining pairs are mined, every validation and test connectivity from both evaluation benchmarks is excluded from source and target structures. Generated intermediates with an excluded connectivity are also removed.

B.2 Exact-Fingerprint PubChem Pairs

For each formula, every valid one-edit product of every remaining PubChem structure is generated and identical exact products are merged. Two PubChem structures connected directly define a directed D1 pair. Two structures whose expansions meet at a shared product define a D2 pair when no direct transition exists. All valid first actions that realize a shortest direct connection or enter a shortest shared intermediate are retained as positives.

Pairs are grouped by source molecule. Half of the sampled examples come from contrast groups containing up to four D1 or D2 targets for the same source, prioritizing different sets of optimal first edits and a mixture of distances. The other half selects one pair from each sampled group to broaden coverage across formulas and source molecules, preferring a D1 target when present and otherwise using a D2 target. Each example uses the exact target fingerprint.

The mined corpus contains 986,681,148 directed source–target examples. Pretraining samples 125 million examples with a 50:50 contrast/coverage allocation. Contrast groups contribute at most four examples and coverage groups one.

B.3 Target-Conditioned D1–D3 Supervision

A distance shell contains states at a given shortest-path distance from the target. For a fixed target tt, define these shells and optimal first-action sets as

𝒟k​(t)\displaystyle\mathcal{D}_{k}(t) ={m:dtrain​(m,t)=k},\displaystyle=\{m:d_{\mathrm{train}}(m,t)=k\}, (10)
𝒜+​(m,t)\displaystyle\mathcal{A}^{+}(m;t) ={a∈𝒜(m):T(m,a)∈𝒟k−1(t)},m∈𝒟k(t),k≥1.\displaystyle=\{a\in\mathcal{A}(m):T(m,a)\in\mathcal{D}_{k-1}(t)\},\quad m\in\mathcal{D}_{k}(t),\ k\geq 1.

Here dtraind_{\mathrm{train}} uses the target class and training exclusions defined in Appendix A.2. Thus 𝒟0​(t)\mathcal{D}_{0}(t) contains the atom-renumbered versions of the reference target graph.

For the D1–D3 corpus, containing molecules with at most 35 heavy atoms, each chosen training target is expanded through two edits. States are matched by the literal bond-and-hydrogen graph up to atom renumbering. Held-out intermediates are excluded during construction, so the resulting shells are complete in the admissible training graph. Reusing these target neighborhoods avoids expanding every PubChem source through two steps.

Same-formula, target-excluded PubChem sources matching the target’s D1 or D2 shell receive the corresponding distance. Every source is expanded once and its products are matched to the target shells. For a source outside the two-step neighborhood, a valid join to the D2 shell gives a three-step path after reversing the target-side path and mapping its atom indices to those of the source-side meeting state. Shorter shell membership is checked first, so the joined path certifies distance three to the chosen training goal. Every retained path is replayed forward under the edit rules and exclusions described in Appendix A.3.

For a source m∈𝒟k​(t)m\in\mathcal{D}_{k}(t), every valid first action entering the complete 𝒟k−1​(t)\mathcal{D}_{k-1}(t) shell is positive. All such first actions are retained for each selected training pair, with a replayed path witnessing each one.

Larger molecules.

For molecules with more than 35 heavy atoms, we construct a separate D1–D2 corpus to avoid the cost of exhaustive two-step target expansion. We enumerate the one-edit neighbors of each target and each same-formula PubChem source. A direct source–target connection gives D1 supervision. If no direct connection exists, a shared one-edit neighbor gives a shortest two-edit path. All source edits entering such shared neighbors are retained as positive actions, and the corresponding paths are replayed and verified. Thus, one-step expansion on each side supplies supervision at distances one and two without a target D2 shell.

Training observations.

D3 sources are capped independently for each target spectrum by

ND3keep=min⁡(ND3,max⁡(50,ND2)).N_{\mathrm{D3}}^{\mathrm{keep}}=\min\!\left(N_{\mathrm{D3}},\max(50,N_{\mathrm{D2}})\right). (11)

The D3 sets contain 378,563 source–target pairs for NPLIB1 and 1,677,732 for MassSpecGym. After pairing these with the target spectra, the cap retains 155,625 and 6,486,972 training observations, respectively. Membership is selected by descending MIST Bernoulli agreement for each spectrum, so spectra of the same target can select different D3 sources. All available D1 and D2 observations are retained.

MIST predicts the target fingerprint from the spectrum, formula, and formula-based peak annotations. The target structure supplies the shortest-path labels. Training excludes source–target pairs at distance zero and mixes D1–D3 examples for molecules with at most 35 heavy atoms with D1–D2 examples for molecules with more than 35 heavy atoms, using the batch schedules in Appendix D.

Appendix C Fingerprint Correspondence Details

The candidate fingerprint is a binary radius-two Morgan fingerprint with 4,096 hashed bits, bond types enabled, and chirality disabled (Rogers and Hahn, 2010). Each of the 128 fingerprint tokens encodes a bit’s identity, evidence type, target probability, candidate presence, and uncertainty and discrepancy features. We initially allocate 48 tokens to high-probability bits missing from the candidate, 48 to present bits with low predicted support, and 32 to present bits with high predicted support. Unfilled slots are filled from the remaining bits by confidence ranking.

The numerical features for a selected bit are

(qi,xi,qi​(1−xi),(1−qi)​xi,qi​xi,qi−xi,h⁡(qi)),(q_{i},x_{i},q_{i}(1-x_{i}),(1-q_{i})x_{i},q_{i}x_{i},q_{i}-x_{i},h(q_{i})),

where h⁡(q)=−q​log⁡q−(1−q)​log⁡(1−q)h(q)=-q\log q-(1-q)\log(1-q) is Bernoulli entropy, with h⁡(0)=h⁡(1)=0h(0)=h(1)=0. The discrepancy feature is signed.

The occurrence map retains every environment that generates each present bit. Radius-zero membership contains only the center atom. Radius-one and radius-two membership expand through the candidate adjacency and include the corresponding heavy bonds. These relations connect fingerprint evidence to atom and directed-bond tokens in the policy. Atom relations distinguish centers and other members at each radius from atoms outside the environment. Bond relations record how many endpoints belong to an environment and whether the bond itself belongs. Missing bits have a separate relation code because they have no occurrence in the candidate.

Appendix D Training Protocol

D.1 MIST Encoders and Input Processing

We use the released FRIGID MIST encoders mist_canopus.pt for NPLIB1 and mist_msg.pt for MassSpecGym. Each benchmark uses one fixed MIST encoder for all training and evaluation spectra. NPLIB1 uses public formula-only peak assignments. MassSpecGym training uses formula-only subformula assignment with 15 ppm tolerance. Protonated evaluation spectra use 20 ppm on both benchmarks. Sodiated MassSpecGym evaluation uses 15 ppm. Peak assignment and fingerprint prediction use the spectrum and formula. Sodiated inference uses the same MassSpecGym encoder with corrected padding and pairwise formula masks, a single square-root intensity transform, the raw Top-60 peaks, and all peaks retained after annotation. Fingerprint prediction uses the sodium adduct. The navigation policy does not take adduct as an input. Adduct-dependent evidence enters through the MIST fingerprint probabilities.

D.2 Network Configuration

All reported fingerprint policies use the same architecture. The embedding width is 256, the feed-forward width is 512, and every attention block uses eight heads. The target fingerprint encoder has two self-attention layers. The molecular encoder has six layers before the two atom–fingerprint cross-attention layers and two layers afterward. Directed bond representations use two self-attention and two fingerprint cross-attention layers. Residual and attention dropout are both 0.1. Atom and bond cross-attention gates and the global target gate are initialized with logit −2-2. Collision energy is not used.

Action heads concatenate directed-bond representations, action-type embeddings, and global molecular features before an MLP. Type A averages four equivalent endpoint orderings. Type B first constructs a hydrogen-transfer representation from donor and recipient atom states and the global state, combines it with directed-bond representations, and averages two orderings. The averaged action representation is projected to a logit.

D.3 PubChem Pretraining

Pretraining uses four H100 GPUs with distributed data parallelism, global batch size 256, and AdamW with learning rate 4×10−44\times 10^{-4}, weight decay 10−210^{-2}, and β=(0.9,0.999)\beta=(0.9,0.999). The learning rate follows cosine decay to zero, starting at the specified rate. Gradient norm is clipped at 1. We use full-precision training, one batch per optimizer step, and random seed 42. The run processes 125 million examples in 488,282 optimizer steps, saving checkpoints at 20 evenly spaced training milestones. Downstream training begins from the checkpoint after 37,499,904 examples, selected by validation Hit@1. We initialize the policy weights from this checkpoint and reset the optimizer, learning-rate schedule, and random states before fine-tuning.

D.4 Target-Conditioned Fine-Tuning

Fine-tuning minimizes Equation 4 and alternates batches from the D1–D3 set (at most 35 heavy atoms) and the D1–D2 set (more than 35 heavy atoms). NPLIB1 uses a 63:1 batch ratio, and MassSpecGym uses a 15:1 ratio. After removing distance-zero pairs, the combined sets contain 314,220 training observations for NPLIB1 and 13,412,519 for MassSpecGym. NPLIB1 trains for three epochs with 5,746 steps per epoch, and MassSpecGym trains for one epoch with 221,855 steps. The reported NPLIB1 checkpoint is from step 8,619, halfway through epoch two. The MassSpecGym checkpoint is from the end of its training epoch.

Both models use one H100, batch size 64, learning rate 5×10−55\times 10^{-5}, AdamW with weight decay 10−210^{-2} and β=(0.9,0.999)\beta=(0.9,0.999), and cosine decay to zero from the initial learning rate. Gradient norm is clipped at 1. We use full precision, one batch per optimizer step, seed 42, and two data loader workers with unpinned batches.

Appendix E Search Algorithm

Valid-action enumeration checks bond-order bounds and heavy-atom connectivity using temporary adjacency arrays. Search materializes product states and constructs RDKit molecules for fingerprinting only for selected top-PP actions. These proposals can later be removed by duplicate/visited checks or beam pruning. Trajectories use policy log probability to preserve sequences of learned edit choices, which need not monotonically improve the current molecule’s fingerprint agreement.

Appendix F Evaluation Protocol and Baseline Comparisons

F.1 Conventions

Unless stated otherwise, GEMS uses up to K=5K=5 MIST-ranked, target-excluded PubChem starts, P=B=16P=B=16, D=3D=3, λ=16\lambda=16, and the reported checkpoint for each benchmark. Query-level results use all 803 NPLIB1 and 17,556 MassSpecGym test queries. MassSpecGym results pool 14,066 protonated and 3,490 sodiated spectra. Queries without starts count as failures. With PubChem initialization, these are 17 NPLIB1 and 200 MassSpecGym queries (129 protonated and 71 sodiated). Appendix H.3 gives the corresponding counts for generated pools.

Reach is the fraction of queries whose retained candidate pool contains a structure with the target’s InChIKey14. It does not depend on ranking and is an upper bound on Hit@kk. Per-seed reach, used in Appendix I, is the fraction of seed–target pairs whose own retained lineage contains the target. Queries without starts contribute no pairs, and queries with more starts receive more weight.

Results at a depth DD below the searched maximum are prefixes of longer searches, with candidates and consensus votes restricted to states retained by depth DD. A target first recovered at depth DD shows a path of DD edits, but the beam may have discarded a shorter one.

Labels such as MIST and Exact FP name the fingerprint used for navigation, ranking, or both. Exact FP is computed from the target structure. It is an oracle diagnostic that is unavailable at inference. Starting sets are fixed across corresponding MIST and exact-fingerprint conditions. Ranked starting sets are selected with MIST. Each training setting uses one random seed. The random-five comparison in Appendix H.1 reports repeated starting-set selections.

F.2 Structural Metrics and Published Baselines

Tables 3 and 4 give the complete published comparisons. NPLIB1 values come from FRIGID Table 1. MassSpecGym values come from MassSpecGym in the Wild Table 9, with FRIGID-base from FRIGID Table 1. We use the corrected MolForge results. MS-GPT (published) provides contextual comparisons (Zhao et al., 2026), with a different NPLIB1 split from ours. For numerical comparisons and refinement experiments, we use MS-GPT (ours), our best-effort reproduction retrained on the same benchmark splits after correcting the MIST attention masking issue described below. This reproduction has not been validated by the original authors. The reproduction uses the same full test sets and FRIGID-compatible structural metric implementation as GEMS. The NPLIB1 adapter checkpoint was selected on its 396 validation spectra, and the MassSpecGym checkpoint by validation cross-entropy.

MIST masking in MS-GPT.

The released MS-GPT implementation retains the MIST padding-mask issue documented in MassSpecGym in the Wild (Liu et al., 2026, Section 6.1.1).22 2 Code inspected at MS-GPT commit f2c844e. Padded tokens can contribute to attention, making fingerprint predictions depend on batch padding. GEMS excludes padded tokens from attention. The effect of the released masking code on MS-GPT’s reported accuracy has not been measured.

GEMS structural metrics use the ranked top-ten unique InChIKey14 candidates and include every test query. We reuse FRIGID’s implementation with RDKit 2026.3.5, myopic_mces 1.2.2, and PuLP 3.3.2. Molecules are converted through InChI, tautomer-canonicalized using FRIGID’s two-transform canonicalizer, and stripped of stereochemistry. Tanimoto uses binary radius-two Morgan fingerprints with 2,048 bits. For each query, Top-kk Tanimoto is the maximum similarity among its first kk candidates, averaged over all queries.

MCES (maximum common edge subgraph) distance measures differences in molecular bonding under the best correspondence between atoms of the same element, accounting for bond order. Lower values indicate closer structural agreement, including when a candidate is not an exact match.

We report thresholded MCES with threshold 15. FRIGID’s evaluator removes invalid or disconnected structures and duplicate InChIs from the first ten ranked candidates, preserving order without backfilling. Thresholded scoring can return lower bounds instead of exact distances. If canonicalization or MCES computation fails, the evaluator substitutes a bond-count score: the sum of target and candidate bond counts, or twice the target bond count. For each query, Top-kk MCES is the minimum returned score among the first kk remaining candidates, capped at 100 and averaged over all test queries. Queries without eligible candidates receive MCES 100 and Tanimoto zero. In our best-effort MS-GPT reproduction, 106 NPLIB1 and 3,295 MassSpecGym queries have no eligible candidates after structural preprocessing. Their MCES-100 penalties contribute 13.20 and 18.77, respectively, to the reported mean MCES.

The full results show the same pattern as Table 1: GEMS improves exact-match accuracy and Top-10 Tanimoto over the baselines evaluated on the same splits. FRIGID has lower MCES on NPLIB1. On MassSpecGym, GEMS reduces both MCES measures relative to FRIGID, while FOAM has lower Top-10 MCES (6.06 versus 8.26).

Appendix G Learning the Navigation Policy

G.1 Pretraining and Supervision

Table 5 compares random-weight and trained policies under the same MIST-guided search and λ=16\lambda=16 ranking. The random-weight policy uses the reported architecture without training and gives 4.61±2.904.61\pm 2.90% Hit@1 and 8.30±5.298.30\pm 5.29% reach on NPLIB1 across three weight initializations (mean ±\pm sample standard deviation), well below every trained NPLIB1 policy. Training improves performance under this fixed proposal and beam budget.

PubChem pretraining alone gives 28.89% Hit@1 on NPLIB1 without downstream fine-tuning, exceeding supervised training from scratch at 28.02%, although its Hit@10 and reach are lower. Fine-tuning adds 0.75 percentage points in Hit@1, 3.99 in Hit@10, and 7.72 in reach. It therefore improves identification as well as recovery. This contrast combines downstream training with adaptation from exact target fingerprints to MIST predictions.

Pretraining followed by fine-tuning outperforms supervised training from scratch in Hit@1, Hit@10, and reach on both benchmarks. The supervised models use the same benchmark-specific navigation examples and validation-selected checkpoints. From-scratch training uses six epochs on NPLIB1 and two on MassSpecGym, with an initial learning rate of 10−410^{-4} and cosine decay to zero without warmup on both benchmarks.

Shortest-path supervision versus REINFORCE.

We compare training from scratch with shortest-path supervision against REINFORCE using exact-target-fingerprint rewards on NPLIB1. The matched recipe uses the same source–spectrum training examples, source-batch schedule, global batch size of 64, and optimizer schedule. REINFORCE samples 32 three-edit trajectories per source. Rewards measure improvement in the best Bernoulli agreement with the exact target fingerprint along a trajectory, divided by 100, with a leave-one-out baseline across trajectories. Policy inputs remain MIST predictions. The training schedule specifies 34,476 updates over six epochs, with four validation evaluations per epoch. Both selected checkpoints are at step 27,293, with supervised checkpoint selection based on λ=16\lambda=16 validation Hit@1.

Shortest-path supervision exceeds REINFORCE in Hit@1, Hit@10, and reach (Table 5). Matching the update and source-exposure schedules does not match GPU-hours or establish variability across training runs. The comparison does not isolate the effect of retaining multiple optimal actions rather than one.

G.2 Learned Search versus Enumerate & Score

Table 6 reports the accuracy and cost of each depth-three configuration. At P=B=4P=B=4, GEMS gives 27.65% Hit@1 on NPLIB1 and 29.18% on MassSpecGym, with processing times of 81.11 and 1,456.71 seconds. This setting costs less than width sixteen, but recovers fewer targets. At the same beam width four, E&S reaches 54.17% of NPLIB1 targets and 44.24% of MassSpecGym targets, compared with 49.07% and 41.35% for GEMS. GEMS has higher Hit@1 on both benchmarks at this width and reduces processing time by factors of 31.1 and 60.0, respectively. E&S has higher NPLIB1 Hit@10.

Increasing the learned beam to sixteen raises reach to 57.78% and 46.88%. At this width, GEMS exceeds every tested E&S width in Hit@1, Hit@10, and reach. Compared with the widest tested E&S beam (B=4B=4), GEMS reduces reported runtime by factors of 12.6 on NPLIB1 and 21.4 on MassSpecGym.

Appendix H Where Search Starts

H.1 PubChem Starting Sets

Table 7 compares query-level identification and recovery across four NPLIB1 starting sets at depths three, five, and ten. The full-catalog and sampled-250 settings select up to five starts by MIST agreement, using either the complete same-formula PubChem pool or a uniform 250-candidate draw. Random starts are the first up to 100 candidates of that draw before fingerprint sorting. The fixed random-five condition uses their first five starts. The same trained checkpoint and P=B=16P=B=16 are used throughout. MIST and exact-fingerprint conditions share the same starts, and each uses its stated fingerprints for both navigation and ranking. Candidates and consensus votes are restricted to the corresponding depth and starting set.

Start quality.

Under MIST guidance, full-catalog MIST selection gives the strongest D3 results among the tested initializations. Ranking within a 250-candidate sample lowers Hit@1 from 29.64% to 26.15% and reach from 57.78% to 50.44%. Up to 100 random starts nearly match full-catalog reach at 57.66%, but identify fewer targets, with 25.53% Hit@1.

Depth and identification.

Deeper search partly compensates for weaker starts. At D10, the fixed random-five setting achieves 22.29% Hit@1 and 40.85% reach, still below the full-catalog ranked setting at D3. At D10, the random-100 setting reaches more targets than the ranked setting (66.00% versus 59.90%), but identifies fewer (28.89% versus 29.64% Hit@1).

Exact guidance.

With exact fingerprints, the fixed random-five setting at D10 nearly matches full-catalog ranked reach at D3 (72.60% versus 72.85%). Exact-guided search from up to 100 random starts recovers the target for 89.91% of queries by D10. These starting sets therefore contain useful edit paths that MIST-guided search does not fully exploit.

Repeated random-five selection.

Across ten runs drawing up to five starts from the same fixed random-100 pool, D3 Hit@1 is 11.41±0.73%11.41\pm 0.73\%, Hit@10 is 20.40±0.74%20.40\pm 0.74\%, and reach is 23.79±1.00%23.79\pm 1.00\% (mean ±\pm sample standard deviation). These runs use different subsets from the fixed five-start prefix in Table 7.

H.2 Starts Filtered by Similarity to the Target

Target-excluded PubChem starts can still include close analogs of the target. Motivated by the analysis of close analogs in pretraining data by Liu et al. (2026), we test sensitivity to similar structures among inference-time starts. We exclude candidates whose Tanimoto similarity to the target is at or above each cutoff, using radius-two, 2,048-bit Morgan fingerprints after the molecular standardization described in Appendix F.2. In a separate condition, we exclude all target-specific connectivity groups identified as one-edit neighbors by exhaustive enumeration. Both conditions retain target-connectivity exclusion. We then select up to five remaining candidates from the full same-formula catalog by MIST agreement. The checkpoint, search settings, and final ranking remain unchanged.

Results.

Accuracy falls as stricter similarity cutoffs are applied (Table 8). At a cutoff of 0.7, the threshold used for close analogs in MassSpecGym in the Wild (Liu et al., 2026), GEMS gives 27.90%/46.45% Hit@1/Hit@10 on NPLIB1 and 23.93%/31.75% on MassSpecGym, above FRIGID’s 25.03%/33.37% and 18.29%/22.00% (Table 1). MassSpecGym is more sensitive to the filter, losing about 6.3 Hit@1 points at 0.7 compared with 1.7 on NPLIB1. On NPLIB1, Hit@1 falls below FRIGID’s only at a cutoff of 0.5 (21.92%), while Hit@10 remains higher (36.36% versus 33.37%). At this cutoff, additional edit rounds raise NPLIB1 Hit@1 from 9.34% at D=1D=1 to 19.05% at D=2D=2 and 21.92% at D=3D=3.

With up to five MIST-ranked starts and P=B=16P=B=16, the D1/D2/D3 Hit@1 values are 27.02%/29.39%/29.64% on NPLIB1 and 30.09%/30.43%/30.22% on MassSpecGym without Tanimoto filtering. At cutoff 0.7, they are 22.79%/27.27%/27.90% and 18.75%/22.76%/23.93%, respectively. The D1–D2 gains are therefore 4.48 and 4.02 percentage points after filtering, compared with 2.37 and 0.34 without it; the D2–D3 gains are 0.62 and 1.17, compared with 0.25 and −0.21-0.21. Gains are computed from hit counts before rounding.

With every one-edit neighbor removed, no target is recovered at D=1D=1. Every target recovered by D=3D=3 is therefore reached through two or three edits. GEMS gives 25.53%/42.22% Hit@1/Hit@10 on NPLIB1 and 22.44%/29.57% on MassSpecGym, still above FRIGID on both benchmarks. Increasing depth from two to three raises Hit@1 from 24.16% to 25.53% on NPLIB1 and from 20.31% to 22.44% on MassSpecGym. With target exclusion alone, the corresponding Hit@1 values change from 29.39% to 29.64% on NPLIB1 and from 30.43% to 30.22% on MassSpecGym. These depth comparisons use up to five starts and P=B=16P=B=16.

Additional starts give larger identification gains under stricter similarity filtering. Increasing the maximum number of starts from five to twenty raises NPLIB1 Hit@1 by 0.75 points without filtering and by 2.12 points at a cutoff of 0.5, and Hit@10 by 1.99 and 5.35 points, respectively. Reach rises by about eight to nine points at every cutoff.

H.3 Generated Starting Pools and Refinement

For both FRIGID and MS-GPT, we select up to five executable same-formula candidates by MIST Bernoulli score, retaining the target when present. The original-ranking rows in Table 10 preserve each generator’s output order. Selected (D0) evaluates the chosen starts, and GEMS (D3) adds states retained during three edit rounds from those same starts. Both use MIST fingerprints and λ=16\lambda=16 ranking, with P=B=16P=B=16 for search. All 803 NPLIB1 and 17,556 MassSpecGym queries remain included, counting queries without executable starts as misses.

FRIGID candidate pools.

The NPLIB1 FRIGID-base pool is the initial round of the same run that produces the final FRIGID pool. Its 65,151 candidates precede all ICEBERG refinement. FRIGID selects up to twelve parents by its own ranking in each of 24 refinement rounds, producing eight masked variants per parent and adding 32 fresh samples. Missing refinement slots are filled with fresh samples. GEMS and FRIGID therefore share the initial generated pool, while parent selection, ranking, and computational budgets differ. For further refinement, GEMS selects from the top 128 saved candidates per query after the 24 FRIGID refinement rounds. The original FRIGID row reports identification accuracy only because the full cumulative pool was not saved. There are 45 NPLIB1 queries without executable FRIGID-base starts and 23 without executable refined FRIGID starts. MassSpecGym includes 474 queries for which FRIGID-base outputs are unavailable.

MS-GPT candidate pools.

We use outputs from our best-effort corrected and retrained MS-GPT reproduction (Appendix F.2), applying the same MIST-based selection and GEMS refinement procedure. There are 128 NPLIB1 and 3,633 MassSpecGym queries without executable selected starts.

Proximity of generated starts.

Table 9 compares the three NPLIB1 starting pools. D0 checks whether a selected start already matches the target, and D1 exhaustively enumerates every valid one-edit product. D2/D3 combine this coverage with saved MIST- and oracle-guided paths, giving lower bounds on the fraction of queries with a start within that many edits. Among queries without a correct selected start, three-edit coverage is at least 292/611 (47.79%) for FRIGID-base, 275/561 (49.02%) for refined FRIGID, and 240/582 (41.24%) for MS-GPT. Queries without starts remain included. These conditional sets differ between generators. The counts establish proximity of the selected starts, independently of final ranking.

Refinement results.

Table 10 compares the original generator rankings, selected starts, and GEMS refinement. Three edit rounds improve Hit@1, Hit@10, and reach over the selected-start baseline for every evaluated generator pool. On NPLIB1, GEMS exceeds our FRIGID run’s original Hit@1 of 24.03%, reaching 28.02% from its initial pool and 28.27% from its refined pool. GEMS also improves on the original ranking of our best-effort MS-GPT reproduction, raising Hit@1 from 21.05% to 26.28% on NPLIB1 and from 23.23% to 25.56% on MassSpecGym. These results use MIST predictions for both navigation and ranking.

H.4 Oracle Guidance from Generated Starts

Table 11 replaces navigation and ranking evidence with exact target fingerprints for the FRIGID and MS-GPT starts. Seed selection still uses MIST, so the starting pools are identical to the corresponding refinement runs. These are oracle diagnostics. Oracle D3 results are prefixes of completed ten-round searches, as are the corresponding MIST results for MS-GPT. The FRIGID MIST comparisons use standalone three-round searches.

With the starting pools fixed, exact fingerprints improve recovery and identification from both FRIGID pools on NPLIB1 and from MS-GPT on both benchmarks. On NPLIB1, Hit@1 rises from 28.02% to 57.91% for FRIGID-base and from 28.27% to 61.52% for refined FRIGID. Navigation and ranking change together in these comparisons. FRIGID-base oracle reach is 60.15%, while the 60.27% proximity bound in Table 9 also includes exhaustive one-edit coverage and paths witnessed by other searches.

Generated starting pools often contain candidates connected to the target by short edit paths. However, proximity alone does not ensure successful refinement: MIST-guided search misses some reachable targets, and final ranking does not consistently place recovered targets first. Exact-fingerprint interventions improve both recovery and identification from the same starting pools.

Appendix I Search Width and Depth

I.1 Width versus Depth

The NPLIB1 grid varies P=BP=B and depth using the reported model and fixed ordered starting sets: up to five MIST-ranked starts or up to 100 random starts per query. Depths are prefixes of ten-round searches. Table 12 reports query-level identification, while Figure 4 and Table 13 report per-seed reach, the fraction of individual seed–target searches that recover the target. Per-seed reach separates individual search success from the number of opportunities per query, although queries with more starts receive more weight and the starting distributions differ.

Width versus depth under MIST.

From the reference setting P=B=D=3P=B=D=3, we compare widening to P=B=10P=B=10 at D=3D=3 with deepening to D=10D=10 at P=B=3P=B=3. Both expanded settings retain at most B​D=30BD=30 search states plus the initial structure per seed before final deduplication. This matches the maximum retained-candidate budget, while actual unique candidate counts and computation can differ. From ranked starts, widening raises Hit@1 from 28.02% to 29.89%, compared with 29.02% for deepening. Per-seed reach similarly rises from 32.43% to 38.79% with widening and 37.22% with deepening. From random starts, the ordering reverses: widening raises Hit@1 from 24.91% to 25.90%, while deepening raises it to 29.39%. Per-seed reach rises from 5.58% to 7.10% and 20.38%, respectively. Hit@10 follows the same ordering for both starting sets. Ranked starts therefore benefit more from exploring alternatives within a short search, whereas random starts benefit more from extending trajectories in this comparison.

Exact fingerprint evidence changes the tradeoff.

With exact fingerprints, deepening is more beneficial for both starting sets. From ranked starts, reference Hit@1 is 68.99%, compared with 68.87% for widening and 78.46% for deepening. From random starts, the corresponding values are 66.25%, 66.50%, and 84.18%. Per-seed reach and Hit@10 support the same ordering. Deeper search can thus yield substantially greater gains with more informative fingerprint evidence. Exact fingerprints replace both navigation and ranking inputs here, so this comparison does not isolate their individual contributions.

Diminishing returns in identification.

From ranked starts under MIST, widths ten and sixteen differ by at most 0.50 percentage points in Hit@1 at the reported depths D∈{1,3,5,10}D\in\{1,3,5,10\}. Recovery still improves: at D=3D=3, per-seed reach rises from 38.79% to 41.31% between these widths. At width sixteen, extending D=3D=3 to D=10D=10 further raises per-seed reach to 45.99%, while Hit@1 and Hit@10 remain at 29.64% and 50.81% at the two endpoints. Additional search therefore continues to improve recovery without necessarily improving identification.

I.2 Recovery by Depth on Both Benchmarks

Table 14 reports query-level recovery by depth on both benchmarks, using the reported trained policies, up to five MIST-ranked PubChem starts, and P=B=16P=B=16. The retained paths show that many target-excluded retrieved isomers are close to an accepted target. With MIST guidance, at least one start reaches the target within a single edit for 51.56% of NPLIB1 queries and 43.30% of MassSpecGym queries. Recovery rises to 57.78% and 46.88% by depth three. These measurements depend on the candidate pool, independently of final ranking.

On both benchmarks, additional depth yields substantially larger recovery gains with exact fingerprint evidence. Extending search from D3 to D10 adds 2.12 percentage points of reach on NPLIB1 and 0.94 on MassSpecGym under MIST guidance. With exact fingerprints, the same extension adds 12.08 and 8.96 points.

Additional recovery does not consistently improve top-ranked identification. We compare depth-three and depth-five prefixes of the same searches, using the candidates and lineage votes retained through each depth. Under MIST guidance, extending search from D3 to D5 raises NPLIB1 reach from 57.78% to 58.78%, while Hit@1 changes from 29.64% to 29.76%. On MassSpecGym, reach rises from 46.88% to 47.30%, while Hit@1 decreases from 30.22% to 29.88%.

I.3 Witnessed Paths and Certified Distances

A recovered target establishes a valid edit path, but the first recovery depth need not be the shortest possible distance. Certifying that distance requires both a verified path and exhaustive exclusion of shorter paths. Figure 1 illustrates a certified three-edit example. Table 14 reports witnessed paths across the benchmarks, where this certification procedure has not been applied to every starting seed. Failure to recover a target with a finite beam leaves its distance unresolved.

We measure deval​(s,t)d_{\mathrm{eval}}(s,t) from the exact initial seed state, accepting any endpoint whose InChIKey14 matches the reference target. For a target-excluded seed, exhaustive forward search through two edits tests every reachable state for a match. A first match at depth one or two certifies that distance. If neither depth contains a match, the distance is at least three.

To search for a three-step path, we also expand the reference target by one edit. The InChIKey14 values in that neighborhood select promising seed-reachable states at depth two. We then expand those states forward from their actual bond-and-hydrogen configurations. A path is accepted only when its endpoint matches the target InChIKey14 and all three edits replay successfully. Combined with the two-step lower bound, this certifies distance three.

The target-side filter can miss paths ending at other accepted target structures. When no verified path is found, the lower bound remains three and the exact distance is unresolved.

Appendix J Fingerprint Evidence in Navigation and Ranking

J.1 Fingerprint Interventions with PubChem Starts

Table 15 reports fingerprint interventions with and without consensus. Its λ=16\lambda=16 rows give the numerical results for Figure 3.

Navigation.

With λ=16\lambda=16 and MIST ranking, replacing the navigation fingerprint with the exact target fingerprint raises reach from 57.78% to 72.85% on NPLIB1 and from 46.88% to 56.07% on MassSpecGym. Hit@1 increases from 29.64% to 33.25% and from 30.22% to 33.82%, respectively. Recovery therefore improves more than top-ranked identification.

Ranking.

Many recovered targets are not placed first by MIST ranking. With the MIST-guided candidate pools fixed, replacing only the ranking fingerprint raises Hit@1 from 29.64% to 56.66% on NPLIB1 and from 30.22% to 45.12% on MassSpecGym. These values approach the corresponding reach of 57.78% and 46.88%. Candidate pools and consensus counts remain unchanged, so the improvement comes from selecting among already recovered candidates rather than additional search.

Replacing both navigation and ranking fingerprints raises Hit@1 further, to 68.99% on NPLIB1 and 53.09% on MassSpecGym. Together, these oracle interventions show scope to improve both target recovery and selection from the recovered pool, with the starting sets and trained checkpoints held fixed.

J.2 Effect of Consensus

We select λ=16\lambda=16{} by MassSpecGym validation Hit@1 across both adducts and use it for both benchmarks.

Consensus reorders a fixed candidate pool without changing reach. It raises Hit@1 from 28.02% to 29.64% on NPLIB1 and from 29.47% to 30.22% on MassSpecGym (Table 15). The improvement in NPLIB1 Hit@10 is smaller, from 50.56% to 50.81%.

Among the tested interventions, consensus gives its largest Hit@1 gains with exact navigation and MIST ranking: 3.86 percentage points on NPLIB1 and 2.63 on MassSpecGym.

Removing consensus leaves the main conclusion of the fingerprint experiment unchanged (Table 15). With the MIST-guided pools fixed, exact-fingerprint ranking raises Hit@1 from 28.02% to 55.54% on NPLIB1 and from 29.47% to 44.76% on MassSpecGym. Using exact fingerprints for both navigation and ranking raises these values to 67.62% and 51.04%. These comparisons use the same seeds, checkpoint, and candidate pools as the λ=16\lambda=16 conditions. Only the consensus term is removed.

J.3 Reranking with Predicted Spectra

We test whether predicted spectra provide complementary ranking evidence by reranking the fixed top-ten lists from the main GEMS configuration. ICEBERG (Goldman et al., 2024) predicts a spectrum for each candidate using the benchmark-specific checkpoints released with FRIGID. We add a spectral score S⁡(m)S(m) to the GEMS score, giving R⁡(m,q)+β​S​(m)R(m;q)+\beta S(m), while keeping λ=16\lambda=16. The metric, energy aggregation, and β\beta are selected by validation Hit@1, with β∈{0,4,8,16,32,64,128}\beta\in\{0,4,8,16,32,64,128\}.

NPLIB1 selects β=128\beta=128 and experimental intensity coverage, the fraction of observed intensity matched by predicted peaks. MassSpecGym selects β=32\beta=32 and cosine similarity of square-root intensities. Both use one-to-one peak matching within 20 ppm and exclude precursor and above-precursor peaks. For NPLIB1, scores use matched recorded collision energies when available and otherwise average over 10–90 eV in 10 eV increments. MassSpecGym uses the nearest grid energy to the recorded value, or 40 eV when energy is unavailable.

The validation-selected spectral scores improve Hit@1 on both benchmarks (Table 16), showing that forward spectral predictions complement fingerprint-based ranking. Substantial identification error remains within the fixed candidate lists. All test queries remain in the denominators. Hit@10 and full-pool reach are unchanged because reranking preserves candidate membership and cannot rescue targets outside the top ten. Appendix K.2 reports the additional prediction cost.

Appendix K Runtime Measurements

At K=5K=5, P=B=16P=B=16, and D=3D=3, GEMS takes 200.12 seconds end to end on NPLIB1, the median of three runs over all 803 test spectra, or 0.249 seconds per spectrum. This wall time includes process startup, model and data loading, spectrum preprocessing, peak annotation, MIST prediction, fresh fingerprint database construction, retrieval, search, final ranking, and output writing. Post-hoc accuracy evaluation and correctness audits are excluded, as are queue waiting and prior PubChem download and catalog ingestion. The MassSpecGym measurement is accumulated processing time of 4,091.00 seconds, or 0.233 seconds per spectrum, and excludes startup and file I/O. Table 17 reports these runtimes alongside their component costs.

K.1 Search Timing Boundaries

Search timers start after the main-process model has been initialized and include worker initialization, warm-up, and search until results are returned in memory. NPLIB1 processes the full test set in one task. MassSpecGym is divided into sixteen contiguous groups, with at most two tasks running concurrently. Reported time is the sum of all sixteen task durations. Each task uses 32 physical CPU cores, 32 workers, and 192 GiB RAM. Learned search also uses one H100.

K.2 Pipeline Timing Boundaries

The NPLIB1 P=B=16P=B=16 GEMS timer starts at process launch and stops after ranked predictions have been written and the process exits. It measures one continuous execution from available raw spectra and formula catalogs. All three runs start fresh processes and reload the models; filesystem caches are not flushed. The end-to-end value is used consistently in Tables 6 and 17.

The component rows in Table 17 isolate in-memory processing costs. Preprocessing parses and normalizes spectrum peaks; annotation assigns molecular subformulas; MIST predicts fingerprint probabilities. Database construction freshly fingerprints validated candidate SMILES, and retrieval selects the starting structures. Final ranking includes consensus scoring, molecule validation, connectivity deduplication, and worker startup and shutdown. Input-component and ranking times are medians of three repetitions, as is the NPLIB1 P=B=16P=B=16 search time; other search times retain the recorded task measurements.

Continuous end-to-end timing is available only for NPLIB1 GEMS at P=B=16P=B=16. The remaining entries in Table 6 report accumulated processing costs for the shared inputs, each method’s search, and final ranking, excluding startup, file I/O, and post-hoc evaluation. Thus the NPLIB1 comparison charges loading and output overhead to GEMS alone. MassSpecGym search costs cover sixteen tasks, with final ranking measured separately over the full cohort on 32 CPU workers.

FRIGID-base generation.

A separate FRIGID-base generation run over all 803 NPLIB1 spectra took 5,353 seconds on one H100. This standalone timing is distinct from the run supplying the initial pool for the paired FRIGID/GEMS refinement comparison. FRIGID’s published accuracy in Table 1 includes subsequent ICEBERG refinement.

FRIGID with ICEBERG refinement.

Our NPLIB1 run takes 94,408 seconds, approximately 26.2 hours, for all 803 test spectra. It uses one H100, 32 allocated CPU cores, and 128 GB host memory, with 128 attempted samples per spectrum per round and initial generation followed by 24 refinement rounds. The final saved ranking gives Hit@1/Hit@10 of 24.03%/33.13%. This benchmark wall time includes model and data loading, MIST prediction, generation, ICEBERG subprocesses, per-round ranking and evaluation, and output writing. GEMS’s end-to-end runtime is 200.12 seconds, approximately 3.3 minutes, using one H100, 32 physical CPU cores, and 192 GiB host memory. It includes loading and writing through the final ranked predictions, with post-hoc evaluation excluded as described above.

ICEBERG reranking.

Producing the test prediction caches for Appendix J.3 takes 16 minutes 58 seconds on one H100 for NPLIB1 and 9 minutes 59 seconds across eight H100s for MassSpecGym, totaling 17.0 and 79.2 GPU-minutes, respectively. These prediction-job times include model setup and output writing, but exclude queue waiting, input preparation, GEMS search, and coefficient selection. CPU spectral scoring adds approximately 15 and 81 seconds, respectively. The caches support multiple scoring and energy choices. The selected rules require only 60,622 of 69,425 cached conditions on NPLIB1 and 106,676 of 355,912 on MassSpecGym.

K.3 Illustrative Neighborhood Enumeration

For a 32-heavy-atom NPLIB1 molecule, one-edit enumeration produced 1,904 distinct connectivities in 2.10 seconds. Extending to two edits processed 4.57 million valid proposals and found 1.72 million additional connectivities in 41 minutes 39 seconds on one CPU worker.33 3 The example is C24​H30​F2​O6\mathrm{C}_{24}\mathrm{H}_{30}\mathrm{F}_{2}\mathrm{O}_{6}, InChIKey14 FEBLZLNTKCEFIT. A third exhaustive round would expand 2.20 million atom-aligned states, with an upper bound of 5.68 billion raw edit proposals before validity filtering. This rapid neighborhood growth motivates GEMS’s selective edit expansion and bounded beam at each depth.

Appendix L Illustrative Search Trajectories

Figures 5 and 6 show MIST-guided paths from selected PubChem seeds at certified distances one, two, and three on each benchmark. Distance refers to the displayed seed, not the closest seed in the query’s starting pool. Each sequence follows a retained seed lineage to its first target hit. All displayed edits were replayed from the saved initial state, checking formula and atom-valence preservation and the final target InChIKey14. The shorter-path exclusion procedure is described in Appendix I.3. These examples were selected after evaluation for illustration.

Longer paths under predicted fingerprints.

Figures 7 and 8 compare guidance from MIST predictions and exact target fingerprints. Within each pair, the initial seed state, trained checkpoint, search widths, and final target structure are identical. The first retained target path from that seed takes five versus three edits on NPLIB1 and six versus three on MassSpecGym. The certified distance is three in both cases, so the MIST-guided paths contain two and three additional edits, respectively. These comparisons concern navigation; they do not depend on the target’s final rank or imply that another seed could not reach it sooner.

A longer path from a random start.

Figure 9 follows one of 100 random PubChem starts for an NPLIB1 query. The retained path opens and reconnects rings before reaching the target at its tenth edit. This is an observed path length; its shortest possible distance has not been certified. Other seeds for this query recover the target earlier.
